Dean–Jett–Fox Model Implementation in JavaScript

Overview

The Dean–Jett–Fox (DJF) model describes a DNA-content histogram as the sum of:

  1. A Gaussian G1 peak
  2. A broadened S-phase distribution
  3. A Gaussian G2/M peak

For asynchronous populations, the underlying S-phase population is represented by a second-degree polynomial.

For synchronous populations, the Fox extension adds a Gaussian-shaped cohort within S phase. This allows the model to represent a concentrated group of cells progressing through S phase after release from an arrest.

A practical implementation should use one nested model:

  • Asynchronous model: G1 + polynomial S phase + G2/M
  • Synchronous model: G1 + polynomial S phase + synchronized S-phase Gaussian + G2/M

Fit the asynchronous model first. Fit the synchronous extension afterward and retain it only when the added component provides a meaningful, penalized improvement in fit.

6. JavaScript Normal-Density Function

/**
 * Normal probability density:
 *
 *                  1               -(x - mean)^2
 * phi(x; mu, sd) = ----------- exp(-----------------)
 *                   sd*sqrt(2pi)        2*sd^2
 */
export function normalPdf(x, mean, sd) {
  if (!Number.isFinite(x)) {
    throw new TypeError("x must be finite.");
  }

  if (!Number.isFinite(mean)) {
    throw new TypeError("mean must be finite.");
  }

  if (!Number.isFinite(sd) || sd <= 0) {
    throw new RangeError("Standard deviation must be positive.");
  }

  const z = (x - mean) / sd;

  return (
    Math.exp(-0.5 * z * z) /
    (sd * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI))
  );
}

7. Constructing the Discrete S-Phase Grid

The S-phase integral can be approximated numerically by dividing S phase into many small positions.

/**
 * Construct discrete masses representing the underlying,
 * unbroadened S-phase population.
 *
 * Asynchronous:
 *
 * qA(z) = w0(1-z)^2 + 2*w1*z*(1-z) + w2*z^2
 *
 * Synchronous Fox extension:
 *
 * qF(z) = qA(z) + AF*phi(z; zF, sigmaF)
 */
export function makeSPhaseGrid(params, steps = 128) {
  const {
    mu1,
    ratio,
    nSPoly,
    nSBump = 0,
    sShape,
    bumpMean = 0.5,
    bumpSd = 0.1,
  } = params;

  if (!Number.isInteger(steps) || steps < 8) {
    throw new RangeError(
      "S-phase grid must contain at least 8 steps.",
    );
  }

  if (
    !Array.isArray(sShape) ||
    sShape.length !== 3 ||
    sShape.some(value => !Number.isFinite(value) || value < 0)
  ) {
    throw new TypeError(
      "sShape must contain three nonnegative values.",
    );
  }

  const mu2 = ratio * mu1;
  const width = mu2 - mu1;

  if (!(width > 0)) {
    throw new RangeError(
      "The G2/M mean must be greater than the G1 mean.",
    );
  }

  const positions = new Float64Array(steps);
  const polynomialShape = new Float64Array(steps);
  const bumpShape = new Float64Array(steps);
  const masses = new Float64Array(steps);

  let polynomialSum = 0;
  let bumpSum = 0;

  for (let j = 0; j < steps; j++) {
    // Midpoint of one normalized S-phase interval.
    const z = (j + 0.5) / steps;

    // u = mu1 + z(mu2 - mu1)
    const u = mu1 + z * width;

    positions[j] = u;

    // Quadratic Bernstein basis.
    const b0 = (1 - z) ** 2;
    const b1 = 2 * z * (1 - z);
    const b2 = z ** 2;

    // qA(z)
    const polynomial =
      sShape[0] * b0 +
      sShape[1] * b1 +
      sShape[2] * b2;

    polynomialShape[j] = polynomial;
    polynomialSum += polynomial;

    // AF*phi(z; zF, sigmaF), normalized later by area.
    if (nSBump > 0) {
      const bump = normalPdf(
        z,
        bumpMean,
        bumpSd,
      );

      bumpShape[j] = bump;
      bumpSum += bump;
    }
  }

  if (!(polynomialSum > 0)) {
    throw new RangeError(
      "The S-phase polynomial has zero area.",
    );
  }

  for (let j = 0; j < steps; j++) {
    const polynomialMass =
      nSPoly *
      polynomialShape[j] /
      polynomialSum;

    const bumpMass =
      nSBump > 0 && bumpSum > 0
        ? nSBump * bumpShape[j] / bumpSum
        : 0;

    masses[j] =
      polynomialMass +
      bumpMass;
  }

  return {
    positions,
    masses,
    mu2,
  };
}

8. Broadening the S-Phase Grid

/**
 * Discrete approximation of:
 *
 * S(x) = integral q(u)*phi(x; u, CV*u) du
 *
 * grid.masses[j] contains the cell mass associated
 * with underlying DNA position u[j].
 */
export function convolvedSPhaseDensity(
  x,
  grid,
  cvS,
  minimumSd = 1e-9,
) {
  if (!Number.isFinite(cvS) || cvS <= 0) {
    throw new RangeError(
      "S-phase coefficient of variation must be positive.",
    );
  }

  let density = 0;

  for (let j = 0; j < grid.positions.length; j++) {
    const u = grid.positions[j];

    // sigmaS(u) = CV*u
    const sd = Math.max(
      cvS * u,
      minimumSd,
    );

    density +=
      grid.masses[j] *
      normalPdf(x, u, sd);
  }

  return density;
}

9. Evaluating the Complete DJF Histogram

/**
 * Evaluate expected counts for every histogram bin.
 *
 * M(x) = G1(x) + S(x) + G2(x)
 */
export function expectedDJFHistogram(
  binCenters,
  binWidth,
  params,
  sGridSteps = 128,
) {
  const {
    mu1,
    ratio,
    cv1,
    cv2,
    nG1,
    nG2,
  } = params;

  if (!(binWidth > 0)) {
    throw new RangeError(
      "Histogram bin width must be positive.",
    );
  }

  const mu2 = ratio * mu1;

  // sigma1 = CV1*mu1
  const sd1 = cv1 * mu1;

  // sigma2 = CV2*mu2
  const sd2 = cv2 * mu2;

  const sGrid = makeSPhaseGrid(
    params,
    sGridSteps,
  );

  const expected =
    new Float64Array(binCenters.length);

  for (let i = 0; i < binCenters.length; i++) {
    const x = binCenters[i];

    // G1(x) = N1*phi(x; mu1, sigma1)
    const g1Density =
      nG1 *
      normalPdf(x, mu1, sd1);

    // G2(x) = N2*phi(x; mu2, sigma2)
    const g2Density =
      nG2 *
      normalPdf(x, mu2, sd2);

    // S(x) = sum_j mj*phi(x; uj, CV1*uj)
    const sDensity =
      convolvedSPhaseDensity(
        x,
        sGrid,
        cv1,
      );

    // lambda_i = binWidth*M(x_i)
    expected[i] = Math.max(
      1e-12,
      binWidth *
        (
          g1Density +
          sDensity +
          g2Density
        ),
    );
  }

  return expected;
}

Relationship to the Formula

The component calculations implement:

The total density is:

A density is converted into an expected histogram count by multiplying by bin width:

The JavaScript expression:

binWidth * (
  g1Density +
  sDensity +
  g2Density
)

implements this equation.

Multiplication by bin width is important. Without it, changing the number or width of histogram bins changes the apparent component areas.

10. Constraining Optimization Parameters

An optimizer should operate on unconstrained real-valued variables and transform them into biologically valid DJF parameters.

function sigmoid(x) {
  if (x >= 0) {
    const e = Math.exp(-x);
    return 1 / (1 + e);
  }

  const e = Math.exp(x);
  return e / (1 + e);
}

function interpolate(min, max, fraction) {
  return min + fraction * (max - min);
}

/**
 * Softmax with the first logit fixed at zero.
 *
 * This removes the redundant direction produced by
 * adding the same constant to every softmax logit.
 */
function anchoredSoftmax(freeLogits) {
  const logits = [0, ...freeLogits];
  const max = Math.max(...logits);

  const values = logits.map(
    value => Math.exp(value - max),
  );

  const sum = values.reduce(
    (total, value) => total + value,
    0,
  );

  return values.map(
    value => value / sum,
  );
}

/**
 * Asynchronous theta length: 8
 * Synchronous theta length: 11
 */
export function decodeDJFParameters(
  theta,
  {
    totalCount,
    mu1Min,
    mu1Max,
    synchronous,
  },
) {
  const expectedLength =
    synchronous ? 11 : 8;

  if (theta.length !== expectedLength) {
    throw new RangeError(
      `Expected ${expectedLength} parameters, ` +
      `received ${theta.length}.`,
    );
  }

  const mu1 = interpolate(
    mu1Min,
    mu1Max,
    sigmoid(theta[0]),
  );

  const ratio = interpolate(
    1.75,
    2.25,
    sigmoid(theta[1]),
  );

  const cv1 = interpolate(
    0.005,
    0.20,
    sigmoid(theta[2]),
  );

  const cv2 = interpolate(
    0.005,
    0.20,
    sigmoid(theta[3]),
  );

  // Two optimizer variables define three positive,
  // normalized Bernstein weights.
  const sShape = anchoredSoftmax([
    theta[4],
    theta[5],
  ]);

  if (!synchronous) {
    const fractions = anchoredSoftmax([
      theta[6], // G2/M
      theta[7], // polynomial S phase
    ]);

    return {
      mu1,
      ratio,
      cv1,
      cv2,
      sShape,

      nG1:
        totalCount * fractions[0],

      nG2:
        totalCount * fractions[1],

      nSPoly:
        totalCount * fractions[2],

      nSBump: 0,
      bumpMean: 0.5,
      bumpSd: 0.1,
    };
  }

  const fractions = anchoredSoftmax([
    theta[6], // G2/M
    theta[7], // polynomial S phase
    theta[8], // synchronized S-phase cohort
  ]);

  return {
    mu1,
    ratio,
    cv1,
    cv2,
    sShape,

    nG1:
      totalCount * fractions[0],

    nG2:
      totalCount * fractions[1],

    nSPoly:
      totalCount * fractions[2],

    nSBump:
      totalCount * fractions[3],

    // Keep the Fox Gaussian away from the exact
    // G1 and G2/M locations.
    bumpMean: interpolate(
      0.05,
      0.95,
      sigmoid(theta[9]),
    ),

    bumpSd: interpolate(
      0.015,
      0.25,
      sigmoid(theta[10]),
    ),
  };
}

11. Poisson-Deviance Objective

Histogram bins contain counts. A Poisson likelihood is therefore generally more appropriate than unweighted least squares.

The Poisson deviance is:

where:

  • is the observed count in bin
  • is the expected DJF count

When , the contribution is:

export function poissonDeviance(
  observed,
  expected,
) {
  if (observed.length !== expected.length) {
    throw new RangeError(
      "Observed and expected histograms " +
      "must have equal lengths.",
    );
  }

  let deviance = 0;

  for (let i = 0; i < observed.length; i++) {
    const y = observed[i];

    const lambda = Math.max(
      expected[i],
      1e-12,
    );

    if (y > 0) {
      deviance +=
        2 *
        (
          lambda -
          y +
          y * Math.log(y / lambda)
        );
    } else {
      deviance +=
        2 * lambda;
    }
  }

  return deviance;
}

Relationship to the Formula

For bins containing events:

lambda - y + y * Math.log(y / lambda)

implements:

The final factor of 2 gives the Poisson deviance.

The fitted parameter vector is:

12. Building the Optimizer Objective

export function makeDJFObjective({
  observed,
  binCenters,
  binWidth,
  totalCount,
  mu1Min,
  mu1Max,
  synchronous,
  sGridSteps = 128,
}) {
  return theta => {
    const params = decodeDJFParameters(
      theta,
      {
        totalCount,
        mu1Min,
        mu1Max,
        synchronous,
      },
    );

    const expected =
      expectedDJFHistogram(
        binCenters,
        binWidth,
        params,
        sGridSteps,
      );

    return poissonDeviance(
      observed,
      expected,
    );
  };
}

13. Model Selection for Asynchronous and Synchronous Populations

The synchronous model contains the asynchronous model as a special case:

Therefore, the synchronous model will normally fit at least as well in terms of raw deviance.

A penalty for additional parameters is required.

One option is the Bayesian Information Criterion:

where:

  • = Poisson deviance
  • = number of fitted parameters
  • = number of histogram bins
export function chooseDJFVariant(
  asynchronousFit,
  synchronousFit,
  numberOfBins,
) {
  const asynchronousParameterCount = 8;
  const synchronousParameterCount = 11;

  const asynchronousBic =
    asynchronousFit.deviance +
    asynchronousParameterCount *
      Math.log(numberOfBins);

  const synchronousBic =
    synchronousFit.deviance +
    synchronousParameterCount *
      Math.log(numberOfBins);

  const p = synchronousFit.params;

  const totalModeled =
    p.nG1 +
    p.nG2 +
    p.nSPoly +
    p.nSBump;

  const bumpFraction =
    p.nSBump /
    Math.max(totalModeled, 1);

  /*
   * These thresholds are practical safeguards,
   * not terms in the original DJF equation.
   */
  const useSynchronous =
    synchronousBic <
      asynchronousBic - 10 &&
    bumpFraction >= 0.02;

  return {
    selected:
      useSynchronous
        ? synchronousFit
        : asynchronousFit,

    mode:
      useSynchronous
        ? "synchronous"
        : "asynchronous",

    diagnostics: {
      asynchronousBic,
      synchronousBic,

      deltaBic:
        synchronousBic -
        asynchronousBic,

      bumpFraction,
    },
  };
}

Relationship to the Formula

The synchronous model adds three effective parameters:

  1. : synchronized S-phase abundance
  2. : synchronized cohort position
  3. : synchronized cohort width

A lower BIC is preferred.

The condition:

synchronousBic < asynchronousBic - 10

requires strong evidence favoring the synchronized extension.

The condition:

bumpFraction >= 0.02

requires the synchronized component to represent at least 2% of modeled cells.

These thresholds are configurable safeguards. They are not part of the original DJF formula.

A sample may have been experimentally synchronized without requiring the Fox Gaussian. For example, a population arrested predominantly in G1 may show no separate S-phase cohort.

The selected model describes the histogram shape required by the data, not merely the experimental label.

15. Phase-Fraction Calculation

export function calculateDJFFractions(params) {
  const {
    nG1,
    nG2,
    nSPoly,
    nSBump = 0,
  } = params;

  const total =
    nG1 +
    nG2 +
    nSPoly +
    nSBump;

  if (!(total > 0)) {
    throw new RangeError(
      "The modeled total must be positive.",
    );
  }

  return {
    g1:
      nG1 / total,

    s:
      (nSPoly + nSBump) / total,

    g2m:
      nG2 / total,

    synchronizedS:
      nSBump / total,
  };
}

Relationship to the Formula

The returned values implement:

Multiply each by 100 to report percentages.

16. Component Curves for Plotting

For visualization, return the individual expected curves as well as the total.

export function expectedDJFComponents(
  binCenters,
  binWidth,
  params,
  sGridSteps = 128,
) {
  const mu2 =
    params.ratio * params.mu1;

  const sd1 =
    params.cv1 * params.mu1;

  const sd2 =
    params.cv2 * mu2;

  const sGrid =
    makeSPhaseGrid(
      params,
      sGridSteps,
    );

  const g1 =
    new Float64Array(binCenters.length);

  const s =
    new Float64Array(binCenters.length);

  const g2m =
    new Float64Array(binCenters.length);

  const total =
    new Float64Array(binCenters.length);

  for (let i = 0; i < binCenters.length; i++) {
    const x = binCenters[i];

    g1[i] =
      binWidth *
      params.nG1 *
      normalPdf(
        x,
        params.mu1,
        sd1,
      );

    s[i] =
      binWidth *
      convolvedSPhaseDensity(
        x,
        sGrid,
        params.cv1,
      );

    g2m[i] =
      binWidth *
      params.nG2 *
      normalPdf(
        x,
        mu2,
        sd2,
      );

    total[i] =
      g1[i] +
      s[i] +
      g2m[i];
  }

  return {
    g1,
    s,
    g2m,
    total,
  };
}

18. Numerical Optimization

The DJF objective is nonlinear and does not have a simple closed-form solution.

Possible JavaScript optimizers include:

  • Nelder–Mead
  • Powell optimization
  • BFGS or L-BFGS with numerical gradients
  • Differential evolution
  • CMA-ES
  • A global search followed by local optimization

A robust approach is:

  1. Generate biologically informed starting values.
  2. Fit from several perturbed starting points.
  3. Retain the converged result with the lowest deviance.
  4. Reject fits with invalid values or excessive boundary contact.
  5. Compare asynchronous and synchronous models only after both have been optimized adequately.

The S-phase convolution is usually the most expensive calculation.

19. Web Worker Architecture

The fit should run inside a Web Worker so repeated convolution and optimization do not freeze the interface.

The UI thread should:

  1. Build or receive the DNA histogram.
  2. Send counts, bin centers, bin width, and options to the worker.
  3. Display progress.
  4. Receive the selected model and component curves.
  5. Render the results.

The worker should:

  1. Initialize and fit the asynchronous model.
  2. Calculate asynchronous residuals.
  3. Initialize the Fox Gaussian from the residuals.
  4. Fit the synchronous model.
  5. Compare both models.
  6. Return parameters, fractions, diagnostics, warnings, and curves.

Example request:

worker.postMessage({
  type: "fit-djf",

  histogram: {
    counts,
    binCenters,
    binWidth,
  },

  initialization: {
    mu1,
    mu1Min,
    mu1Max,
  },

  options: {
    fitSynchronous: true,
    sGridSteps: 128,
    optimizerStarts: 10,
  },
});

Example response:

self.postMessage({
  type: "djf-fit-complete",
  result: fitResult,
});

Example progress response:

self.postMessage({
  type: "djf-fit-progress",
  stage: "synchronous-fit",
  completedStarts: 4,
  totalStarts: 10,
});

20. Components Outside the Core DJF Model

The core DJF model should not be forced to absorb every histogram event.

Debris and Sub-G1 Events

Debris and sub-G1 events can create a left-side shoulder or spike.

They should be:

  • Removed by QC, or
  • Represented with a separate debris component

They should not be absorbed by the S-phase polynomial.

Aggregates and Polyploid Events

Doublets, aggregates, and polyploid populations may create peaks beyond G2/M.

They should be:

  • Removed through singlet discrimination, or
  • Modeled as separate aggregate components

They should not be treated as normal G2/M cells.

Background

A small background component may be useful when the histogram contains a broad baseline not explained by biological phases.

Possible background forms include:

  • Constant background
  • Exponential debris term
  • Broad low-amplitude Gaussian

Any added component increases model flexibility and should be penalized during model selection.

21. Recommended Fit Warnings

The implementation should return warnings when:

  • G1 is not clearly detected
  • G2/M is not clearly detected
  • The fitted G2/G1 ratio is near a boundary
  • or is near a boundary
  • The synchronized bump is near or
  • The synchronized bump width is near a boundary
  • The synchronized bump duplicates G1 or G2/M
  • The optimizer fails to converge
  • Different optimizer starts produce substantially different solutions
  • The fitted S-phase fraction is implausibly small or large
  • Residual structure remains after fitting
  • Debris or aggregate contamination is visible
  • Too few singlet events remain for stable fitting

Example:

const warnings = [];

if (params.ratio < 1.77 || params.ratio > 2.23) {
  warnings.push(
    "The fitted G2/G1 ratio is near its allowed boundary.",
  );
}

if (
  params.nSBump > 0 &&
  (
    params.bumpMean < 0.08 ||
    params.bumpMean > 0.92
  )
) {
  warnings.push(
    "The synchronized S-phase cohort is close to a phase boundary.",
  );
}

if (!fit.converged) {
  warnings.push(
    "The optimizer did not converge.",
  );
}

22. Important Interpretation Limits

The synchronized Fox Gaussian identifies a concentrated population within the DNA-content interval between G1 and G2/M.

It does not, by itself, prove:

  • Experimental synchronization
  • A particular arrest mechanism
  • A specific replication rate
  • Cell-cycle direction
  • Entry into or exit from S phase

DNA content alone cannot distinguish a cohort moving forward through S phase from one with similar DNA content for another reason.

Time-series context is needed to interpret movement of the synchronized cohort.

For an arrest-and-release experiment, the fitted values can be tracked over time:

A generally increasing is consistent with progression from early toward late S phase.

However, each time point should not necessarily be fitted independently without regularization. Joint or sequential fitting can improve stability.

23. Optional Time-Series Extension

For synchronous release experiments, neighboring time points can share or constrain parameters.

Examples:

  • Similar across time points
  • Similar across time points

  • Nonnegative cohort abundance

The core single-histogram DJF implementation should be completed and validated before adding this time-series layer.

24. Summary

The asynchronous DJF model is:

The synchronous Fox extension is:

In JavaScript:

  1. Represent G1 and G2/M with normalized Gaussians.
  2. Represent asynchronous S phase with a nonnegative quadratic Bernstein polynomial.
  3. Add a normalized Gaussian within S phase for synchronous populations.
  4. Discretize the S-phase interval.
  5. Broaden every underlying S-phase position using .
  6. Sum the broadened S-phase contributions.
  7. Convert density to expected bin counts using bin width.
  8. Fit using Poisson deviance.
  9. Use constrained parameter transformations.
  10. Fit both model variants and use penalized model selection.
  11. Run optimization in a Web Worker.
  12. Keep debris and aggregates outside the core DJF components.
